newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung popularity dips, HK business confidence high.
newsitem.headline: Tung popularity dips, HK business confidence high.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa has suffered a dip in popularity over plans to curb civil rights, but the territory's blue chip companies are taking an upbeat view of life under Chinese rule from July 1.
The latest findings came just 43 days before Hong Kong, a capitalist territory of 6.4 million people, becomes a part of China again, after 156 years as a British colony.
Underlining the impending flag change, a second advance guard of 66 troops from the People's Liberation Army (PLA) arrived on Monday to get future garrison facilities ready.
And, bringing Hong Kong and Beijing ever closer, a new direct train service from the territory to the Chinese capital launched its maiden journey.

An opinion poll published by the South China Morning Post newspaper showed a drop of 5.6 percent in the number of people who said their trust in Tung had grown since he was chosen by a China-controlled committee as future leader Last December.
Some 41.7 percent of respondents in the survey also said they had "less trust" in Tung, a former shipping tycoon.
In a separate poll by Reuters published on Monday, Hong Kong blue chips companies were positive about the business outlook after the handover, set for midnight on June 30.

"Hong Kong will remain an attractive place to do business given its excellent infrastructure as well as its low tax rate and its advantageous location close to China," Cathay Pacific wrote in response to the Reuters questionaire.
Of 11 blue chip companies asked, all said they were positive about Hong Kong's business environment in the next year.
Ten said they were positive about the outlook over five years, while just one company said it was not positive.
Only two respondents said proposals to weaken civil liberties in Hong Kong would hurt their confidence in Hong Kong's future as a business and financial center.
Last month Tung unveiled plans to curb protests and ban foreign funding for political groups in Hong Kong after July 1.
Since then, he has softened the package, although the basic principles in the restrictions remain unchanged and are fiercely opposed by Hong Kong pro-democracy and human rights groups.

Tung was selected to be Hong Kong's first post-handover leader under close Chinese supervision, to succeed colonial Governor Chris Patten and govern Hong Kong as a Special Administrative Region of China with a high degree of autonomy.

Sino-British treaties on Hong Kong's handover are based on a "one country, two systems" formula that promises to leave Hong Kong's capitalist way of life unchanged for the next 50 years, but many in Hong Kong fear communist-style repression.
The South China Morning Post survey found that less people believed Tung would uphold the "one country, two systems" vow.
Some 68.8 percent indicated they had confidence in the pledge, down from 75.9 percent in a similar survey in February.

The poll also showed the Democratic Party, vilified by Chinese communist officials, was still the most popular party in the territory. If people were allowed to vote, the party would get 25.1 percent, far ahead of the second-placed, pro-China Liberal Party with 10.7 percent of the vote.
Voted into office in popular elections that gave them 19 seats in the 60-seat legislature in 1995, Democratic Party legislators will lose their jobs from July 1.
China plans to disband the Legislative Council and replace it with an interim legislature which it appointed in December.
